How does the Sun look like on a Pluto shiny day? Also, would I be able to see other planets if I was standing on Pluto? Like on Earth we can see Venus, Mars and Jupiter?

The sun would appear roughly 250x brighter than the full moon from earth, but you wouldn't feel a ton of heat from it. The the temperatures only rise about ten to twenty degrees during a Pluto day (-380~-370F). It takes 5.5 hours for light from the sun to reach Pluto compared to 8 minutes to reach earth. I doubt you'd be able to see any other planets with the naked eye. Pluto's orbit is on average ~39 AU (1AU = distance from earth to the sun). There's ~9 AU between earth and Saturn and ~30 between Pluto and Saturn. You might catch a peek of Uranus as it comes closest at ~11 AU (even though Neptune is father out on average, Neptune and Pluto have stable orbital resonance that keeps them on opposite sides) but it would be fairly dim itself at ~19 AU from the sun. Keep in mind that orbits are not circular and some of the distances I used are averages.

Frank Pasquale on Big Data - RSA London (6-11-2015) 19 Min.

Description:

We’ve heard a lot about ‘big data’ in the last few years, but who is connecting the dots about what firms are doing with this information?

Hidden algorithms can make or break reputations, decide the destiny of entrepreneurs, or even devastate an entire economy. Shrouded in secrecy and complexity, decisions at major Silicon Valley and Wall Street firms were long assumed to be neutral and technical. But leaks, whistleblowers, and legal disputes have shed new light on automated judgment. Self-serving and reckless behavior is surprisingly common, and easy to hide in code protected by legal and real secrecy. Even after billions of dollars of fines have been levied, underfunded regulators may have only scratched the surface of this troubling behavior. Is it true, for example, that there are no regulations governing how third-party data brokers and marketers assemble and distribute ‘microtargeting lists’? Law professor Frank Pasquale visits the RSA to argue that we all need to be able to know more and to set limits on how big data affects our lives.
